{{short description|Probability theory concept}}
In [[queueing theory]], a discipline within the mathematical [[probability theory|theory of probability]], the '''G/G/1 queue''' represents the queue length in a system with a single server where interarrival times have a general (meaning arbitrary) distribution and service times have a (different) general distribution.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Bhat | first1 = U. N. | chapter = The General Queue G/G/1 and Approximations | doi = 10.1007/978-0-8176-4725-4_9 | title = An Introduction to Queueing Theory | url = https://archive.org/details/introductiontoqu00bhat_435 | url-access = limited | pages = [https://archive.org/details/introductiontoqu00bhat_435/page/n176 169]–183 | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-8176-4724-7 }}</ref> The evolution of the queue can be described by the [[Lindley equation]].<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Foss | first1 = S. | chapter = The G/G/1 Queue | doi = 10.1002/9780470400531.eorms0878 | title = Wiley Encyclopedia of Operations Research and Management Science | year = 2011 | isbn = 9780470400531 }}</ref>

The system is described in [[Kendall's notation]] where the ''G'' denotes a general distribution for both interarrival times and service times and the 1 that the model has a single server.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kendall | first1 = D. G. | author-link1 = David George Kendall| title = Stochastic Processes Occurring in the Theory of Queues and their Analysis by the Method of the Imbedded Markov Chain | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177728975 | jstor = 2236285| journal = The Annals of Mathematical Statistics | volume = 24 | issue = 3 | pages = 338 | year = 1953| url = http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.aoms/1177728975 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Smith | first1 = W. L. | author-link1 = Wally Smith (mathematician)| title = On the distribution of queueing times | doi = 10.1017/S0305004100028620 | journal = [[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]| volume = 49 | issue = 3 | pages = 449 | year = 1953| bibcode = 1953PCPS...49..449S}}</ref> Different interarrival and service times are considered to be independent, and sometimes the model is denoted '''GI/GI/1''' to emphasise this. The numerical solution for the '''GI/G/1''' can be obtained by discretizing the time.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Grassmann |first1=Winfried |last2=Tavakoli |first2=Javad |title=The Distribution of the Line Length in a Discrete Time GI/G/1 Queue |journal=Performance Evaluation |date=June 2019 |volume=131 |pages=43-53}}</ref>

==Waiting time==

[[Kingman's formula]] gives an approximation for the mean waiting time in a G/G/1 queue.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kingman | first1 = J. F. C. | author-link1 = John Kingman| doi = 10.1017/S0305004100036094 | author2 = <!-- (exclude bad crossref data) --> | title = The single server queue in heavy traffic | journal = [[Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society]]| volume = 57 | issue = 4 | pages = 902 | date=October 1961 | jstor = 2984229| bibcode = 1961PCPS...57..902K}}</ref> [[Lindley's integral equation]] is a relationship satisfied by the stationary waiting time distribution which can be solved using the [[Wiener–Hopf method]].<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Prabhu | first1 = N. U. | author-link1 = N. U. Prabhu| chapter = Wiener-Hopf Techniques in Queueing Theory | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-80838-8_5 | title = Mathematical Methods in Queueing Theory | series = Lecture Notes in Economics and Mathematical Systems | volume = 98 | pages = 81–90 | year = 1974 | isbn = 978-3-540-06763-4 }}</ref>

==Multiple servers==

Few results are known for the general G/G/''k'' model as it generalises the [[M/G/k queue]] for which few metrics are known. Bounds can be computed using [[mean value analysis]] techniques, adapting results from the [[M/M/c queue]] model, using [[heavy traffic approximation]]s, empirical results<ref name="gautam">{{cite book | first = Natarajan | last = Gautam | title = Analysis of Queues: Methods and Applications | publisher= CRC Press | year = 2012 | isbn = 9781439806586}}</ref>{{rp|189}}<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Whitt | first1 = W. | author-link1 = Ward Whitt| title = Approximations for the GI/G/m Queue| doi = 10.1111/j.1937-5956.1993.tb00094.x | journal = [[Production and Operations Management]]| volume = 2 | issue = 2 | pages = 114–161 | year = 2009 | url = http://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/ApproxGIGm1993.pdf}}</ref> or approximating distributions by [[phase type distribution]]s and then using [[matrix analytic method]]s to solve the approximate systems.<ref name="gautam" />{{rp|201}}

In a G/G/2 queue with [[heavy-tailed distribution|heavy-tailed]] job sizes, the tail of the delay time distribution is known to behave like the tail of an exponential distribution squared under low loads and like the tail of an exponential distribution for high loads.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Harchol-Balter | first1 = M. |author1-link=Mor Harchol-Balter| chapter = Task Assignment Policies for Server Farms | doi = 10.1017/CBO9781139226424.031 | title = Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems | pages = 408 | year = 2012 | isbn = 9781139226424 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Whitt | first1 = W. | author-link1 = Ward Whitt| title = The impact of a heavy-tailed service-time distribution upon the M/GI/s waiting-time distribution| journal = Queueing Systems | volume = 36 | pages = 71–87 | doi = 10.1023/A:1019143505968 | year = 2000 | url = http://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/impact2000.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Foss | first1 = S. | last2 = Korshunov | first2 = D. | doi = 10.1007/s11134-006-3613-z | title = Heavy Tails in Multi-Server Queue | journal = [[Queueing Systems]]| volume = 52 | pages = 31 | year = 2006 | arxiv = 1303.4705}}</ref>
